items.description: Telecel Ghana has rewarded a lucky subscriber, Eric Ayamgash, with a Hyundai Creta at the end of the 15th cycle of its Dream Car promotion. The initiative forms part of the telecommunications company’s efforts to reward customer loyalty and support the aspirations of its subscribers. Senior Manager in charge of Mobile Data at Telecel Ghana, Carlos Asare Oppong, says the promotion reflects the company’s commitment to creating rewarding experiences and helping customers achieve their dreams. He disclosed that the latest presentation marks the eighth car awarded under the promotion, in addition to six houses given to winners over the programme’s 15 cycles. “We believe that Ghanaians are very aspirational, and as an aspirational brand, we want to be able to support our customers to achieve their dreams and their goals in life. That is why we launched the Dream Car promotion about 15 cycles ago,” he said. Mr Asare Oppong also announced improvements to the 16th cycle of the promotion, including an additional GH¢100,000 cash prize expected to be awarded towards the end of November or December. He further revealed that the next cycle will feature a bigger car, urging subscribers to remain active on the network and participate in the promotion for a chance to win. Meanwhile, winner Eric Ayamgash expressed excitement and gratitude to Telecel Ghana, describing his win as a testament to the authenticity of the promotion. He said after failing to win in the previous year’s edition, he was determined to put in more effort in the subsequent cycle. “Last year, I tried but I couldn’t win. When I saw the video of the winner, I said to myself that the next one I’m going to try and put in more effort. God being so good, I was called that I am the winner for this cycle. I just want to say thank you very much, Telecel. I’m so grateful,” he said. Mr Ayamgash encouraged other subscribers to participate, insisting that the promotion is genuine. The Dream Car promotion, which is approved by the National Lottery Authority, gives Telecel subscribers the opportunity to win prizes by participating through the designated USSD platform. Subscribers can dial *2018# on their Telecel SIM cards to take part in the promotion.

items.title: Ghanaian music can go global without copying foreign sounds – King Promise
items.description: Ghanaian Afrobeats and Highlife singer-songwriter King Promise says his ambition is to take Ghanaian music to the global stage without losing the sound and identity that distinguish local artistes from their international counterparts. The Terminator hitmaker said he had previously experimented with music heavily influenced by foreign sounds but eventually realised that Ghanaian artistes should build on their unique strengths rather than imitate what already exists elsewhere. Speaking on Joy FM’s Drive Time with Lexis Bill on Tuesday, October 27, he said his focus had always been on achieving global success while maintaining a strong connection with Ghanaian audiences. “I’d rather them not influencing me so much, rather me influencing the world so much,” he said, referring to the influence of international music on his creative direction. King Promise admitted that there was a period when he was making music driven largely by foreign influences, but he chose not to release those experimental songs. “I was making music that was mainly driven by a lot of foreign influence down home, but that was when I was experimenting. I didn’t drop them,” he explained. He said he subsequently recognised that Ghanaian musicians possessed distinctive musical qualities that could appeal to international audiences. “What they lack in the rest of the world is what we have here. So why would you trade what you have here for what they have?” he asked. According to him, international success should not require Ghanaian artistes to abandon their musical identity in an attempt to appeal to foreign markets. He cited the global popularity of Spanish-language hit Despacito as an example of how music can cross borders without abandoning its original identity. “If Despacito could be a big record in Ghana, why can’t “Mene medofa ahye dam mu” be big in Spain? Or why can’t “Terminator” be played in Singapore?” he said. The singer added that his belief in his music and its potential audience had remained central to his career. “It’s going to work. It has to work. If it doesn’t go this way, we keep going until it goes,” he said. King Promise also discussed the challenge of balancing the tastes of audiences in Ghana with those of listeners abroad. He said he had spent years trying to find a sound that could connect with both markets. He cited songs including Perfect Combi , Paris and Terminator as examples of his efforts to create music with appeal at home and internationally. He also referenced earlier releases such as Tokyo . The singer said he had drawn inspiration from R2Bees, whom he admired while he was in school because of their ability to achieve success both in Ghana and among audiences in the diaspora. He also acknowledged the influence of Nigerian artistes Mr Eazi, Wizkid and Davido, saying their achievements had reinforced his belief that Ghanaian musicians could compete globally. King Promise, who won the Artiste of the Year award, said his international ambitions extended beyond music releases to collaborations and partnerships, including his work with Chelsea Football Club. He maintained that the goal was to help Ghanaian music reach wider audiences while retaining the qualities that make it distinctive.

items.title: I compete with myself, not other artistes – King Promise
items.description: Ghanaian Afrobeats and Highlife singer-songwriter Gregory Bortey Newman, known popularly as King Promise, says he is more focused on improving his own achievements than competing with fellow artistes, describing his approach to the music industry as a continuous pursuit of personal growth. The singer said although competition was a normal part of the music business, comparisons between musicians were often driven by fans rather than the artistes themselves. Speaking on Joy FM’s Drive Time with Lexis Bill on Tuesday, October 27, he said his priority was to build on every milestone in his career rather than become preoccupied with the achievements of others. “I’ve never been but with myself. I’m in my own lane,” he said when asked whether he competed with other musicians. King Promise acknowledged that fans often compared artistes and sought to position their favourites against one another, particularly when awards and career achievements were involved. “It’s normal, you know, I believe like when you’re in contention to be at the apex of your career, and people are doing similar stuff, it might not even be the artists, it might be the fans that will put you against each other,” he said. He added that he preferred to use the achievements of other musicians as motivation rather than allow comparisons to create resentment. “Rather than have it feel like negative competition, if there’s anything that I feel the need to compete is to see someone do something like, ‘Oh, this is nice,’ and I like this. It should inspire me rather than put spite in me,” he explained. The musician cited his relationship with Mr Eazi as an example of how another artiste’s success could motivate him. He said watching his friend achieve international recognition had strengthened his belief in what was possible for Ghanaian musicians. King Promise also referred to Wizkid’s achievement of selling out London’s O2 Arena, saying it inspired him to pursue similar milestones. “You see Wizkid do something like, ‘Ah bro, he sold out the O2, I want to do it too one day.’ Why was it him and it’s not me? That’s my mentality,” he said. He explained that his ambition was to keep identifying new levels to reach, regardless of what he had already accomplished. “I’m like, okay, what can we do next? Well, okay, this went this way, I’ve seen that, okay, it has to go this way next, and that’s really what it is,” he said. The singer also spoke about his friendship with Mr Eazi, whom he has known since around 2012, before either of them had a hit song. According to King Promise, their relationship developed from genuine friendship rather than a deliberate effort to collaborate musically. He said Mr Eazi had influenced him through his directness, confidence and business-minded approach, adding that the two often exchanged ideas beyond music. King Promise said he valued relationships built on genuine connections, citing his longstanding associations with Mr Eazi, R2Bees and Sarkodie. Looking ahead, he told Lexis Bill that he had major plans for his career in Ghana and internationally. He also mentioned new music, future music videos, an upcoming album and his Promise Land event as part of his plans. He further hinted that he might release another song before the end of the year, although he did not confirm a date.

items.title: Who Said It: Marissa Mayer, or Odysseus?
items.description: Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task. Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special. Mayer—the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at Google, where she was the first female engineer—likes cracking a hard problem. But she felt overwhelmed by the range and complexity of potential answers. So Mayer asked her personal A.I. assistant, Dazzle. Within a few seconds, Dazzle delivered an answer. “It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer said. She thought it was perfect. In an attempt to express the blend of bewilderment and despair brought on by this New York Times anecdote , I have concocted a quiz: Which is it—a question the tech industry wants me to ask AI, or something Odysseus asks upon returning to Ithaca after 20 years of absence? Tell me, what is my son like? Who are these people in my house? Are any of these people my son’s friends? Are any of these people my friends? What makes my son smile? What would make a good gift for my son? Do I have anything in common with my son? Would archery be a fun activity to do to impress my family? Is there a quicker route home I could take next time? What would be a nifty surprise for my wife? What activities or items does my wife enjoy? What activity can I do to bond with my wife and son? Does my dog recognize me? Is there something I can feed my elderly dog that will help him live longer? I am told this is my home, but I don’t recognize any of these people in my house, and I don’t know what they want. I am told this is my life, but all of the intimate things that should be the most familiar feel foreign to me. Suggest a fun activity to distract me from the terrifying sense that I have hollowed out my life with my own hands, and that my absence has filled my house with strangers! Is Zendaya Athena?

items.title: Effondrement d’un immeuble à Thiès : le ministère de l’Urbanisme annonce un renforcement des contrôles
items.description: Un immeuble en construction s’est effondré mardi 27 octobre 2026, à proximité de la Brioche Dorée, à Thiès. Le bilan provisoire fait état d’un mort et de deux blessés. Selon le ministère de l’Urbanisme, le bâtiment avait fait l’objet d’un ordre d’arrêt des travaux après la constatation de deux niveaux supplémentaires réalisés sans autorisation. Un mort et deux blessés. C’est le bilan provisoire de l’effondrement d’un immeuble en construction survenu mardi 27 octobre à Thiès, à proximité de la Brioche Dorée. Selon un communiqué du ministère de l’Urbanisme, des Collectivités territoriales et de l’Aménagement des territoires, les trois victimes ont été ensevelies sous les décombres. Deux ont été extraites vivantes avant d’être évacuées vers une structure sanitaire. La troisième a perdu la vie. L’examen du dossier administratif du bâtiment révèle des irrégularités dans l’exécution des travaux. L’immeuble disposait d’une autorisation de surélévation limitée au niveau R+3. Toutefois, lors d’un contrôle effectué le 9 juin 2026, la Division régionale de l’Urbanisme avait constaté que la construction avait atteint le niveau R+5, soit deux étages supplémentaires réalisés sans autorisation. Un ordre d’arrêt des travaux avait alors été matérialisé sur le bâtiment. Les causes de l’effondrement ne sont pas encore établies. Le ministère annonce une expertise technique destinée à déterminer les circonstances du drame. Les investigations porteront notamment sur la structure de l’ouvrage, la capacité portante des fondations et des éléments porteurs au regard des niveaux ajoutés, la qualité des matériaux utilisés ainsi que les conditions d’exécution des travaux. En coordination avec l’autorité administrative, la collectivité territoriale concernée et les services techniques compétents, le ministère prévoit également de veiller à la sécurisation du site, aux vérifications nécessaires et à l’établissement des responsabilités par les instances habilitées. Dans la foulée de cet accident, les contrôles seront renforcés sur les chantiers en cours ainsi que sur les bâtiments présentant des signes de dégradation ou d’instabilité. Le ministère rappelle que toute construction doit respecter l’autorisation délivrée, les plans approuvés et les normes techniques en vigueur. Tout ajout de niveaux est soumis à une autorisation préalable, après vérification de la capacité de l’ouvrage existant. Les maîtres d’ouvrage, promoteurs, architectes, bureaux d’études et entreprises sont tenus de se conformer à ces prescriptions, sous peine des sanctions prévues par la réglementation.

items.title: The Limits of Trump’s Midterm Trickery
items.description: For the first time in modern American history, a sitting president is seeking to wield the force of the state to secure an electoral victory for his party. The Trump administration has attempted to undermine the widespread use of mail-in voting; demanded that states hand over voter rolls; threatened to prosecute state and local election officials; refused to rule out the idea of deploying troops or federal agents to polling places; and publicized the dramatic arrests of small numbers of people accused of voting or registering to vote as noncitizens. Many of these efforts have made little headway—either because of the administration’s incompetence, the stubborn lack of factual evidence behind President Trump’s claims of voter fraud, the federal government’s lack of legal authority, or the refusal of courts to go along with Trump’s plans. But Trump may have a different problem on his hands. Polls show Trump’s approval falling to all-time lows in the weeks before Election Day; the percent of voters happy with his performance has now sunk into the 30s. Democrats, meanwhile, appear likely to retake control of the House of Representatives and maybe even the Senate, which last year seemed well out of reach. The polls could be wrong—and high-profile-polling misses of the Trump era are hard to forget. But if the polling is right, the GOP may be in for what George W. Bush, after a disastrous 2006 midterm, ruefully termed a “thumping.” And a thumping, as opposed to a narrower Democratic victory, could render most efforts to suppress turnout irrelevant, and make it far more difficult to implement any more dramatic effort to rig the results. To Trump’s endless frustration, elections in America are organized at the state and local level, with little role for the federal government. In a typical midterm year, almost 470 congressional seats are up for grabs across 50 different states. Though a small number of those races are actually competitive, tinkering with the outcome of the votes would still require meddling with a number of different elections, all run differently, in different jurisdictions, under different laws. A strong night for the Democratic Party would make conjuring an ersatz House majority hard for the same reason that a losing sports team is less able to cheat its way to a victory in a blowout. (Even on a very strong night for the Democrats, the Senate may still be quite a close call.) Tight margins, by contrast, can make an election more vulnerable to efforts to undo the voters’ will. Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 presidential election relied in significant part on tight margins in some swing states, sometimes with only 10,000 or 20,000 votes deciding the winner. In Georgia, the president famously pushed Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find 11,780 votes” to make up his deficit against Joe Biden. As described by both the House January 6 committee’s report and Jack Smith’s indictment of Trump, Trump and his allies used close tallies in swing states, together with the slow counting of mail-in ballots, to engineer doubts over election results and provide Republican members of Congress with the tools to delay the formal counting of the electoral vote on January 6. The attack on the Capitol followed. The memory of January 6, and the entrenchment of the election-denier movement since 2020, has led to speculation—both anxious and enthused—about the possibility of a comparable attack on election results in 2026. If, once most of the results are in, Democrats seem set to eke out a House majority by just a few seats, perhaps committed Trump allies in positions of power could make trouble in a handful of the closest districts. A local election commissioner, say, could refuse to sign off on a Democrat’s narrow victory, or the Justice Department could execute a warrant to seize ballots and thus delay or upend the counting of votes. This could create chaos on January 3, when the new House gathers for the first time: What happens if the contested seats are enough to deny the should-be-majority party the votes it needs to select a new speaker and take control of the chamber? Although this isn’t a foolproof trick for stealing control of the House, such a play could make things very precarious very quickly . But the bigger the majority secured by Democrats, the more difficult it would be for Trump to shave that majority down—the more clerks to convince, warrants to secure, and court rulings to dodge, all over the country. “If there is a House majority in either direction that is 20, 30 seats, I think the likelihood of an attempt to engage in some kind of shenanigans around January 3 is way less than if the majority is two or three seats,” Jonathan Diaz of the Campaign Legal Center commented recently on a preelection panel convened at UCLA’s law school. Other tricks are also less effective when the vote swings heavily in one direction. For example, Trump’s unprecedented push for explicitly partisan off-cycle redistricting may net only a few extra GOP seats rather than the double-digit gains Democratic strategists had once feared. Political constraints matter too. Any scheme to steal the House for the GOP would depend on the willingness of congressional Republicans to vote in lockstep, with no defectors—something that the current fractious House Republican caucus can barely manage. Already, though, Republicans spooked by Trump’s bad poll numbers have begun distancing themselves from him on the campaign trail as they fight to hold on to their seats. Over the summer, Republican politicians and MAGA-friendly media outlets responded coolly to a rambling address by the president casting doubt on election integrity. If the GOP loses the House, how many Republicans concerned about their own political careers would be actually inclined to adopt the fringe message of an ever more unpopular lame-duck president? (Trump has been notably quiet recently about the possibility of running for an unconstitutional third term.) Trump will be hard-pressed to fight against “a clear loss, coupled with the expectation of a clear loss,” Bob Bauer told me. Bauer—a longtime Democratic lawyer who played a central role in the Biden campaign’s fight against Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election—now focuses on bipartisan election-integrity work, alongside Ben Ginsberg, an election lawyer known for his past work representing the Republican Party. In 2020, Bauer said, the additional days required for the presidential race to be called after the polls closed helped fuel Trump’s claims of fraud. But now, broad public dissatisfaction has aligned with dismal polling for the GOP and a growing anticipation among both politicians and the press that Republicans will do poorly. “It would be very difficult in these circumstances, if things turn out that the Democrats do well, for him to suddenly announce that he was denied his landslide by vote rigging,” Bauer told me. Just because such a scheme would be implausible does not, of course, mean that Trump won’t try it. Last week, the Justice Department filed a bizarre lawsuit seeking to preemptively block Alaska from certifying the results of its Senate race—but only if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses. (“The legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen,” wrote the law professor Derek Muller in an analysis of the case.) DOJ also continues to pursue litigation seeking to force California to set aside mail-in ballots to voters whom the federal government claims to have identified as noncitizens. These cases are sloppy, tardy, and almost certainly doomed. But they do have the advantage of helping Trump and his allies build a narrative about the courts blocking Trump’s efforts to ensure a fair election. Likewise, if a Trump-aligned rogue local election official tried to block a Democratic candidate’s victory, whatever he or she concocted as reasoning could provide fuel for election-fraud rumors on the far right, even if the effort—as it likely would—ultimately failed. In a wave election, some races will still be close. They may just be in different states or districts—mostly, more Republican ones—than in a year with more typical political geography. House seats in deep-red areas across the country may be newly up for grabs. In the Senate, races in Texas and Alaska stand out as potential flash points. “Any close race in the Senate is going to be hotly, hotly contested,” Bauer told me. He pointed to the bitter fight between the Democrat Al Franken and the Republican Norm Coleman over the 2008 Senate election in Minnesota, which took months to resolve and ended with the courts upholding Franken’s 312-vote victory. In the final weeks before the midterms, election experts have seemed notably calmer than some of the the anxious rhetoric around Trump’s potential subversion of the vote might suggest. Eight experts interviewed by The New York Times (including Bauer) voiced worries about possible upheaval but overall confidence that officials are prepared to protect the integrity of the elections. The nonprofit publication Votebeat likewise surveyed 31 authorities on election administration and found the group to be wary but “cautiously optimistic” that the midterms will go smoothly. If the elections pass without serious disruption, a hefty margin of victory for the Democratic Party could be partly why. But the fact that such a margin may be needed to avoid chaos is itself sobering. In a healthy democracy, the opposition party should not have to win by enormous numbers to ensure victory, and voters should be able to trust that even a close election will be free and fair.

items.title: MIKTA envoys, FG seek stronger climate finance partnerships ahead of COP31
items.description: By Favour Ulebor, Abuja Diplomats from MIKTA member countries and the Federal government have called for improved access to climate finance, stronger international partnerships and increased investment in practical solutions to help developing countries address climate change. The call was made at a MIKTA roundtable on Climate Finance and Implementation Partnerships in Africa, held on Tuesday in Abuja, ahead of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31, scheduled to hold in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. The discussions brought together representatives of Australia, Türkiye, Indonesia, the Republic of Korea, Mexico, Ethiopia and relevant stakeholders from the climate change sector to examine ways of translating climate commitments into projects that support economic growth, energy access, agriculture and community resilience. Speaking at the meeting, the Australian High Commissioner to Nigeria, Ms Leilani Bin-Juda PSM, said climate action must deliver practical outcomes, particularly for developing countries and communities most vulnerable to its effects. Bin-Juda said many developing countries continued to face difficulties accessing climate finance because of complex applications, fragmented funding systems, reporting requirements and delays. She said Australia was working with Türkiye towards COP31 and with Pacific partners to ensure their priorities were reflected in the global climate discussions. The High Commissioner also highlighted a Pacific-led Action Plan on access to climate finance for Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries, launched at Pre-COP in Fiji on October 8. She said the initiative sought to simplify funding applications, approvals and disbursement, mobilise private investment and strengthen countries’ capacity to develop investment-ready projects. Bin-Juda urged Nigeria to support the initiative, noting that broader international backing would strengthen efforts to make climate finance more accessible and responsive to the needs of vulnerable countries. “For Australia, COP31 is about turning climate ambition into practical outcomes,” she said. The Turkish Ambassador to Nigeria, Mehmet Poroy, said COP31 should focus on implementing existing commitments and ensuring that climate ambitions translated into measurable results. Poroy said African countries needed adequate financial resources, technology, institutional capacity and support for project preparation to implement their national climate plans. He said climate finance should also support development priorities, including energy systems, sustainable agriculture, food security, green industries and climate-resilient cities. The ambassador highlighted Türkiye’s Climate Implementation Bridge initiative, being developed with the United Nations Development Programme, to help developing countries bridge the gap between climate commitments and investment-ready projects. He explained that the initiative was not designed to establish a new fund or replace existing climate finance mechanisms, but to help countries connect their climate priorities with appropriate financing and private capital. Poroy said cooperation between MIKTA countries and African partners could help strengthen implementation as the international community prepares for COP31 and COP32, expected to be hosted by Ethiopia in 2027. Meanwhile, the Indonesian Ambassador to Nigeria, Bambang Suharto, said the scale of investment required to achieve climate targets in developing countries highlighted the need to combine public resources, private investment and international support. He said Indonesia estimated that it would require about $472.6bn to achieve its climate targets, with annual financing needs of approximately $14.5bn through 2030, compared with an annual state budget allocation of about $4.42bn. Suharto said Indonesia was exploring different financing instruments, including green sukuk, blended finance, thematic bonds and concessional funding, to support climate action. He called for existing international climate finance commitments to be delivered and for greater support for project preparation to help countries develop proposals capable of attracting investment. The envoy also highlighted the importance of ocean conservation and coastal resilience, including mangrove restoration, early-warning systems and sustainable fisheries. He expressed Indonesia’s readiness to consult with Nigeria and interested partners on a possible Indonesia-Nigeria Climate Finance and Resilience Partnership, with potential areas of cooperation including climate-resilient agriculture, land restoration, coastal protection, clean energy and green industrialisation. Similarly, South Korea’s Ambassador to Nigeria, Jeong Yoan, outlined opportunities to deepen climate cooperation with Nigeria through renewable energy, agricultural technology, infrastructure and green investment. Jeong said South Korea was committed to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 and had set a 2035 target to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by 53 to 61 per cent compared with 2018 levels. He said Korea’s cooperation with Nigeria included a planned 2026 to 2030 project involving the Korea International Cooperation Agency, KOICA, and the Food and Agriculture Organisation, FAO, aimed at creating green jobs for young people in agriculture and food systems. According to him, the project is expected to support practical training in climate-smart agriculture and digital technology, with the broader objective of improving food security and strengthening resilience. Jeong also identified private investment and a stable investment environment as important factors in mobilising climate finance, noting that clear regulations, transparent procedures and reliable infrastructure could encourage long-term investment. He noted, Nigeria estimated that it would require about $337bn between 2026 and 2035 to meet its climate commitments, underscoring the need for domestic resources, international financing and private-sector participation. The Mexican Charge d’Affaires in Nigeria, Jose Manuel Briseno Flores, also stressed the need to ensure that climate resources translated into practical outcomes, including renewable energy products. He said climate finance should support solutions that could be deployed to address the needs of communities while advancing the transition towards cleaner energy. In her remarks, the Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change, NCCC, Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi, said the country was committed to moving from climate pledges to implementation. Majekodunmi who was represented by the council’s Department of Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, NCCC, Mrs Jummai Vandu said Nigeria supported efforts to turn its Nationally Determined Contributions into bankable, investment-ready projects that could attract financing and deliver measurable results. She identified adaptation finance, decentralised climate action, gender inclusion and a just transition as key priorities for the country. According to her, climate finance must be predictable and accessible to communities facing environmental challenges, while international partnerships should create pathways for states, cities and local governments to implement projects at the subnational level. She also said women and young people should be empowered as decision-makers and direct beneficiaries of climate investments, adding that the transition to clean energy must protect energy security, job creation and economic equity. Majekodunmi said Nigeria was ready to work with MIKTA, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and other international partners to ensure that COP31 produced practical outcomes. Also speaking, the Ambassador of Ethiopia to Nigeria, Legesse Geremew Haile, said Africa faced disproportionate climate vulnerabilities despite contributing marginally to global emissions. He called for direct access to predictable, grant-based financing and technology transfers, noting that African countries needed support to implement their climate priorities. The Ethiopian envoy highlighted his country’s Climate Resilient Green Economy Strategy and Green Legacy Initiative as examples of efforts to combine environmental protection, employment and sustainable development. He said Ethiopia was looking forward to hosting COP32 in 2027, adding that the conference would provide an opportunity to place African development priorities, just energy transitions and loss-and-damage delivery at the centre of the global climate agenda. MIKTA is a cross-regional partnership comprising Mexico, Indonesia, the Republic of Korea, Türkiye and Australia. items.title: UBA Foundation opens 2026 essay competition to promote literacy among SHS students
items.description: The UBA Foundation has opened applications for its 2026 National Essay Competition, seeking to strengthen the writing skills, creativity and critical thinking of senior high school students across Ghana amid concerns about declining literacy skills among young people. The competition offers students an opportunity to develop their writing abilities, express their ideas and compete for financial support towards their tertiary education. Regional Head of Brand, Marketing and Corporate Communications at UBA West Africa, Henry Nii Dottey, said the initiative formed part of the foundation’s efforts to support education and nurture the creative potential of young people. He said the foundation had observed a decline in the literary skills of young people and was using the competition to encourage more students to develop their writing abilities. “This is one of our support initiatives to society. We’ve observed that the literary skills of our young people keep declining. So, one of the things we aim to do is to help improve their creative skills by getting them to write,” he said. Mr Dottey said the competition was open to eligible senior high school students nationwide, with applications for the 2026 edition scheduled to close on November 13. He encouraged students to apply through the UBA Ghana website, stressing that the competition offered an opportunity to strengthen their skills while securing financial assistance for further education. “The competition is open from now until November 13. We want to encourage everybody watching that once you’re in a secondary school in Ghana, you’re eligible. There’s good money to support your tertiary education. You have to apply through the UBA Ghana website,” he said. Previous winner urges students to participate For Stephanie Ewuraabena Aidoo, a winner in the 2024 edition, the competition provided benefits beyond financial support for her university education. She said the experience helped her recognise the value of her voice and build confidence in expressing her ideas. “Aside from the major grants from the UBA Foundation to support my university education, I have learnt to value the power of my voice. I have become more confident in expressing my ideas,” she said. She encouraged students to participate rather than dismiss their chances of winning before applying. “So, to every high school student out there, I’ll encourage you to try. A winning essay begins with trying. Don’t disqualify yourself by thinking you won’t be chosen,” she added. The competition has also attracted interest from students who attended a programme promoting the initiative. Emmanuella, Girls’ Prefect of Achimota Senior High School, said listening to speakers at the event had inspired her and encouraged other students to take advantage of similar opportunities. “The programme has been amazing to the very end. Having to sit through and listen to the encouraging words from every speaker has inspired me. So, I encourage every other student out there that it is necessary,” she said. The UBA Foundation says the competition is part of its broader commitment to education and youth development, with the aim of encouraging more young people to embrace reading and writing and build the communication skills needed to contribute to Africa’s development.

items.title: 4 students, one lady killed in Niger governor’s convoy road crash
items.description: By Clare Nnabuike, Minna Five person, four male students and a young lady have died in a fatal accident involving the Niger state governor Mohammed Umaru Bago’s convoy in Minna, the state capital. The incident happened on Monday at Gidan Mangoro community along the Minna–Bida Road. It followed a head-on collision between a high speeding Hilux van in the convoy of Bago, and a private Peugeot 206 car. The lady identified as Mrs Nafisa was driving the car and died at the spot of the accident. She was said to be a staff of an NGO, and Programme Manager at Labspace, and the Founder of Wosh Mart Service Ltd. A resident of Gidan Mangoro, Abdullahi Musa, told Vanguard that the accident occurred at about 11:35am when the governor was returning from Bida. He and his team paid a condolence visit on the Etsu Nupe and chairman of the Niger state council of traditional rulers Alhaji Yahaya Abubakar over the passage of the Sagi Nupe Hajia Aisha. He said the occupants of the private car driven by Nafisa were suspected to be postgraduate students of the Federal University of Technology, Minna. His words, “The people in the private car died instantly, while those in the government Hilux sustained serious injuries with the driver dying on the spot. Nafisa “The accident was caused by wrongful overtaking by the Hilux in the governor’s convoy. The other car was in its lane when the Hilux rammed into it.” A member of staff of Minna General Hospital, where the victims were rushed to told Vanguard that three people died on the spot while two other people died due to high level of injuries sustain from the crash. “Some of the injured victims were subsequently referred to IBB Specialist Hospital for advanced medical care,” he said. Vanguard gathered that one of the occupants of the Hilux van was a former Niger state local government council chairman who sustained fractures to his legs but was still alive at the time of this report. The Niger State Sector Commander of the Federal Road Safety Corps, FRSC Aishat Sa’adu, confirmed the road crash but said that by the time her officers arrived at the scene, the victims had already been evacuated to the hospital. The Police Public Relations Officer of the Niger state command Superintendent of Police Wasiu Abiodun confirmed the incident and said the accident was under investigation. He did not however give the names or numbers of the deceased. “The accident occured this morning and we are investigating it,” Abiodun said. items.title: GRASAG president calls for sustainable funding for agricultural research in Africa
items.description: The President of the Graduate Students Association of Ghana (GRASAG), Richard Class-Peters, has called for sustainable financing for agricultural research to improve food security, boost local production and support economic growth across Africa. He made the call at the recently concluded World Bank’s Africa Growth and Opportunity – Research in Action (AGORA) 2026 conference in Palermo, Italy. Mr Class-Peters said African countries must increase investment in research and innovation while strengthening farmer cooperatives to improve agricultural productivity and build more resilient food systems. “Sustainable financing for agricultural research is critical to empowering innovation, strengthening farmer cooperatives and transforming local agriculture for food security and economic prosperity in Africa,” he said. He noted that increased funding for agricultural research could help farmers access improved technologies, raise production levels and develop practical solutions to challenges affecting the sector. Mr Class-Peters also stressed the importance of supporting farmer cooperatives, saying they enable farmers to share knowledge, access resources and improve their productivity. “We must empower our local farmers and cooperatives with the knowledge, technology and support they need to produce more and contribute meaningfully to Africa’s economic development,” he said. He added that stronger domestic agricultural production could reduce African countries’ reliance on imported food, create jobs and improve livelihoods, particularly in farming communities. The AGORA 2026 conference focused on how African countries can develop the skills, businesses and systems needed to translate investment into employment and economic growth.

items.title: Andre Ayew donates to Black Challenge ahead of World Cup
items.description: Former Black Stars captain Andre Ayew has donated an undisclosed amount to Ghana’s national amputee football team, the Black Challenge, ahead of the 2026 Amputee Football World Cup in Mexico. Although the amount has not been officially disclosed, sources indicate that the donation is estimated to be between GHS 50,000 and GHS 100,000. Ayew visited the team at their training to offer his support and encourage the players ahead of the tournament, which will take place from 13 to 22 November in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico. “I’m here to support and give you all the love and power that I can give you, and to wish you great luck. I hope that you guys will bring us a medal, but the gold will be better,” he said. Ghana have been drawn in Group D alongside Angola, Colombia and Iraq, with 24 national teams set to compete for the title. The donation adds to the support the Black Challenge have received ahead of their World Cup campaign as they seek to build on Ghana’s reputation in amputee football.

items.title: FG to pay workers N70,000 transport allowance for six months
items.description: …19-month health workers’ arrears By Victor Ahiuma-Young The Federal Government and the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) have reached an agreement on a series of measures aimed at easing the economic difficulties facing workers, including a ₦70,000 transport intervention and the payment of 19 months’ arrears owed to health workers. The resolutions were reached at a conciliation meeting held at the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment on Tuesday, 27 October 2026, following an earlier meeting convened on 22 October. The meetings were organised to address concerns raised by the NLC over the rising cost of living, the implementation of the National Minimum Wage, petroleum pump prices, workers’ welfare and outstanding allowances. Under the agreement, the Federal Government will provide a transport intervention of ₦70,000 across all levels for six months, beginning in November 2026. The government also approved the peculiar allowance with effect from 1 May 2026. Payment of the arrears is expected to begin in November and will be made in three equal monthly instalments. In addition, the 19 months’ outstanding allowances owed to health workers will be paid within three months, beginning in December 2026. The meeting also agreed that the Minimum Wage Negotiation Committee would be constituted and commence work immediately. However, the parties remained divided over the effective date for implementing the new minimum wage. On the issue of tax relief for workers, the meeting resolved that the matter would be referred to the National Executive Council, as taxation is a statutory issue. The Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security has submitted the list of beneficiaries and the cost implications of the proposed hazard allowance for agricultural officers to the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission for verification. The verification is expected to be completed within two weeks, after which the commission will issue an implementation template. Similarly, the NSIWC is expected to complete an updated assessment of the cost implications of the proposed CONHESS adjustment within three weeks. The assessment will enable the Presidential Committee on Salaries to take a decision on the matter. The Federal Government and the NLC urged state and local governments to participate in the intervention process and implement the agreed measures. The parties also agreed to reconvene after one month to review the level of implementation of the resolutions. The agreement was signed on behalf of the federal government by Dr. Muhammad Maigari Dingyadi, Honourable Minister of Labour and Employment, Timi Yakubu, Director-General, Budget, Dr. Garba Abdul S. U., Permanent Secretary (SWO), Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation. For the NLC , its president, Comrade Joe Ajaero; For the Joint National Public Service Negotiation Council (JNPSNC), National Secretary, JNPSNC, Olowoyo Gbenga The post FG to pay workers N70,000 transport allowance for six months appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ghana to review laws to implement Accra Convention – Ofosu-Adjare
items.description: The Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, says Ghana will review its laws to facilitate the implementation of the Accra Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents, a move expected to improve businesses’ access to trade financing. Speaking at the signing ceremony in Accra, she said the Convention would address inequalities in access to credit, particularly for businesses transporting goods by road that often struggle to use cargo as collateral for loans. “There are fewer ways to raise finance for one whose goods are on a truck than one whose goods are on a ship. That is the imbalance this Convention was written to correct,” she said. The Convention introduces a negotiable document of title for goods in transit by road, rail, air or sea, allowing the holder to claim the goods and transfer the associated rights to another party. It also provides protections for buyers and banks that rely on the document in good faith, while recognising electronic cargo documents as having the same legal effect as paper-based versions. Mrs Ofosu-Adjare said the framework could help exporters, manufacturers and small businesses unlock capital tied up in goods in transit and improve their ability to secure financing. “Let me say plainly that this signature is for the exporter whose cargo spoils while paperwork catches up. It is for the manufacturer whose capital sits locked in a container. It is for the small firm that has never been able to borrow against goods on a truck,” she said. Ghana to amend legal framework The Minister said the government would review existing laws on transport, the sale of goods, evidence, electronic transactions and secured lending to ensure they accommodate the new cargo documentation system. She said the process would involve collaboration with the Attorney-General’s Department, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Transport. Mrs Ofosu-Adjare added that Ghana intended to complete the necessary constitutional processes and deposit its instrument of ratification among the earliest signatories. She stressed that signing the Convention was only the first step and that its benefits would depend on effective implementation. “The statute will follow, working with the Attorney-General, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Transport,” she said. Government plans stakeholder collaboration Mrs Ofosu-Adjare called on other countries to sign the Convention and support its implementation to expand trade financing opportunities across different transport systems. She said Ghana would work with institutions including the Ghana Shippers Authority, the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority, the Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority and commercial banks to pilot the use of negotiable cargo documents. The initiative is also expected to support the modernisation of trade documentation, encourage electronic transactions and make it easier for businesses to access credit while their goods are being transported. The Minister said broader participation by other countries would be important to achieving the Convention’s objectives and facilitating trade across borders. “Ghana signs first, but we would be delighted not to sign alone,” she said.

items.title: Ghana’s ambassador to Côte d’Ivoire extends consular outreach to four western towns
items.description: Ghana’s Ambassador to Côte d’Ivoire, Brigadier General Alhassan Abu (rtd), has extended the Embassy’s diaspora engagement and consular outreach programme to Ghanaians living in San Pedro, Sassandra, Grand Lahou and Tabou in western Côte d’Ivoire. The initiative is aimed at strengthening ties with Ghanaians living outside Abidjan, improving access to consular services and addressing concerns affecting their welfare and protection. During engagements with the Ghanaian communities, the Ambassador conveyed the greetings of President John Dramani Mahama and the government, assuring them of the Embassy’s commitment to protecting their interests in the host country. He explained that the Ghana Embassy in Abidjan was responsible for maintaining diplomatic relations between Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, as well as promoting Ghana’s national interests and protecting its citizens. Brigadier General Abu stressed that the welfare and protection of Ghanaians remained a priority for the Mission, saying no Ghanaian should feel abandoned or neglected while living in Côte d’Ivoire. “Hence the doors of the Embassy are open to them at all times,” he said. He outlined the consular services available to Ghanaians, including passport processing and issuance, visas, consular identity cards, attestations, emergency travel certificates and registration of Ghanaian nationals. The Ambassador encouraged Ghanaians to register with the Embassy to enable officials to locate and assist them during emergencies and other crises. He also assured the communities that the biannual Meet Your Ambassador town hall meetings would continue to provide opportunities for the government to explain its policies and programmes while listening to the concerns and grievances of Ghanaians abroad. The Ambassador disclosed that he had led an Embassy delegation to visit Ghanaian nationals detained at the Penitentiary Pole Prison in Abidjan, formerly known as Maison d’Arrêt et de Correction d’Abidjan (MACCA), to provide consular assistance. He said plans were underway to visit other prisons to extend similar support to detained Ghanaians. The visits form part of the Embassy’s broader responsibility to provide consular assistance to citizens facing difficulties in the host country. Brigadier General Abu said the Embassy was working towards establishing a Ghana-Côte d’Ivoire Chamber of Commerce and Industry, alongside plans to organise trade bazaars and cultural events to promote commerce and tourism between the two countries. He cited the participation of 47 Ghanaian small and medium-sized enterprises in the 2026 Semaine Internationale de l’Artisanat de Grand-Bassam (SIAB), held in Côte d’Ivoire from July 30 to August 9, as an example of efforts to expand commercial opportunities. The participation was facilitated by the Ghana Embassy under the auspices of the Ghana Export Promotion Authority (GEPA). On education, the Ambassador said Accra Technical University, Nduom School of Business and Technology, and the University of Cape Coast had signed memoranda of understanding with Côte d’Ivoire’s Ministry of National Education, Literacy and Technical Education to facilitate student exchange programmes. He disclosed that 25 Ivorian students travelled from Abidjan on September 23, 2026, to pursue various programmes at Accra Technical University. The Ambassador also briefed the Ghanaian communities on President Mahama’s Reset Agenda, highlighting developments in the economy, infrastructure, education and healthcare. He cited a reported decline in inflation to 5.2% in September 2026, reductions in public debt, relative price stability and the performance of the cedi as indicators of the government’s economic programme. He also highlighted the phased implementation of the 24-Hour Economy initiative, mentioning the Passport Office, Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority and Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority as institutions operating around the clock. Other initiatives he referenced included the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), the Free Senior High School programme, Operation Recover All Loot (ORAL), and the government’s Big Push infrastructure programme. The Ambassador also pointed to planned road infrastructure, including the Lagos-Abidjan Highway and the proposed Accra-Kumasi Expressway, as part of efforts to improve connectivity and support economic activity. In healthcare, he cited the implementation of primary healthcare initiatives and efforts to expand the local manufacture of medicines and vaccines. These developments, he said, formed part of the government’s broader economic and social transformation agenda. Brigadier General Abu encouraged Ghanaians in Côte d’Ivoire to explore business and investment opportunities in Ghana, saying the government’s policies were intended to create a conducive environment for investment. He also highlighted skills development initiatives, including the Edwumawura and Million Coders programmes, and the support available through the Tree Crops Development Authority for individuals interested in tree-crop farming. He urged members of the diaspora to consider how their skills, experience and investments could contribute to Ghana’s development. Call for unity and security awareness The Ambassador reminded the Ghanaian communities of the longstanding relationship between Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, urging them to protect the cordial ties between the two countries through responsible conduct. He advised Ghanaians to respect Ivorian laws, regulations, customs and traditions, and to live peacefully with their host communities. “United we stand, divided we fall,” he said. He also encouraged them to remain vigilant, be aware of their surroundings and seek travel advice from the Embassy before travelling to neighbouring countries. “The Embassy is at your service 24/7, so do not hesitate to call on the Embassy anytime for assistance or advice when faced with challenges you cannot comprehend,” he added. The outreach forms part of the Ghana Embassy’s efforts to strengthen engagement with citizens across Côte d’Ivoire, improve access to consular support and promote trade, investment and educational cooperation between the two countries.

items.title: ‎NCGC unlocks N64bn credit, vows to end collateral barrier for viable businesses
items.description: ‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ‎ABUJA– THE National Credit Guarantee Company Limited (NCGC) on Tuesday said its guarantees have already unlocked ₦64.13 billion in loans for 174,495 borrowers nationwide, as it intensifies efforts to dismantle the collateral barriers that have long shut viable Nigerian businesses out of formal credit. It said it is supporting an estimated 914,791 direct and indirect jobs within its first 14 months of operation. ‎‎Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Dr. Bonaventure Okhaimo, disclosed this while briefing State House correspondents at the presidential villa, Abuja, on the company’s achievements, challenges and expansion plans. ‎‎The company, which was established by President Bola Tinubu to dismantle longstanding barriers to credit access, has also disclosed that 22,616 Nigerians who had never accessed formal bank credit have secured loans through its intervention, while women now account for 42.7 per cent of beneficiaries. ‎‎Okhaimo, who was accompanied by the Executive Director, Risk Management, Professor Ezekiel Oseni, and Executive Director, Strategy and Operations, Mrs. Tinuola Aigwedo, among others, explained that the company had deployed N30.19 billion in credit guarantees to unlock the N64.13 billion in loans as of October 21, 2026. ‎‎He said the intervention had enabled participating financial institutions to extend loans to previously excluded businesses and individuals, particularly those unable to meet conventional collateral requirements. ‎‎According to him, the initiative has already reached more than 170,000 beneficiaries through 19 participating financial institutions, including commercial and microfinance banks. ‎‎”For every one naira that we give as a credit guarantee to a bank, it creates two naira in loans. That’s the additionality”, Okhaimo explained. ‎‎He stressed that President Tinubu established the company to address a fundamental weakness in Nigeria’s financial system, where otherwise viable businesses were routinely denied credit because they lacked acceptable collateral. ‎‎”The President has said, don’t let a viable Nigerian business suffer because it doesn’t have collateral. He has taken the collateral and given it to the bank. So that’s what we are doing”, he said. ‎‎Explaining the operational model, Okhaimo said NCGC does not lend directly to businesses or individuals but provides guarantees that encourage financial institutions to extend credit to borrowers they would ordinarily consider too risky. ‎‎He said the company currently assumes up to 60 per cent of the credit risk on eligible loans, allowing lenders to relax collateral requirements while retaining responsibility for credit assessment, loan monitoring and recovery. ‎‎According to him, some banks traditionally demand collateral worth more than 150 per cent of the amount being borrowed, a practice that excludes many small businesses despite their commercial viability. ‎‎”What we are saying is, forget about collateral. Do the other due diligence. As long as the customer’s business is viable and the customer has good character, we are willing to support by giving you a credit guarantee that will enable you to give loans to your customers”, he stated. ‎‎On employment generation, the NCGC boss said the company’s interventions had supported 914,791 jobs, comprising direct employment reported by participating banks and indirect employment estimated through recognised development finance multipliers. ‎‎He explained that the indirect employment calculations were based on sector-specific multipliers, including those used by the African Development Bank, with NCGC attributing employment impact according to its share of guaranteed credit risk. ‎‎Speaking on the initiative, Aigwedo said women entrepreneurs remained disproportionately excluded from formal credit because of their limited ownership of assets acceptable as collateral. ‎ ‎ ‎ ‎ ‎ ‎ ‎ ‎ ‎ The post ‎NCGC unlocks N64bn credit, vows to end collateral barrier for viable businesses appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Boris est le Sénégal (Par Khalil DIALLO)
items.description: Qu'appelle-t-on Sénégal aujourd'hui ? Le pays à la deuxième étoile, acquise de haute lutte sur le terrain par la bande à Sadio Mané et toujours disputée devant les tribunaux. Un pays à l'insécurité grandissante, marqué par des homicides sur fond de vols et des féminicides de plus en plus nombreux. La terre à la Teranga éternelle où le débat est rendu difficile par des désaccords politiques. Toutes ces acceptions peuvent être vraies en même temps, et elles le sont, mais celle qui nous intéresse particulièrement est tout autre. À cette question, je réponds, non sans provocation : le Sénégal, c'est Boubacar Boris Diop. À l'occasion de son quatre-vingtième anniversaire, le pays respire littérature et s'offre une pause hors des contraintes socio-économiques pour étudier son œuvre à travers le verbe d'universitaires, d'écrivains, de critiques, d'éditeurs et d'autres personnalités de la République des lettres, parmi lesquelles j'aurais moi-même dû figurer, n'eût été la maladie. Il ne s'agit pas là de rendre un hommage au sens simple et terne du terme, mais d'une tentative d'objectivation de la complexité de l'œuvre qui fait la fierté d'un pays. En portant le Sénégal vers une audience internationale nouvelle à travers Murambi, le livre des ossements, il a permis l'émergence d'une nouvelle génération d'écrivains et nous montrait qu'une autre littérature sénégalaise était possible ; une littérature inclassable, polymorphe, indomptable et sosie du Léviathan. C'est de cette œuvre-là que je me propose de parler, car Boris n'est rien d'autre que ça, ce ça qui a poussé des jeunes de ma génération à chercher plus, plus haut, plus fort, plus dur, ce ça que je nomme le labyrinthe infini d'où coulent sang et larmes, dans lequel il faut à chaque écrivain vivre et créer. Il existe des œuvres qu'il est impossible d’épuiser. Elles sont irréductibles à ce qu'elles racontent : la condition humaine, qu'elles creusent tant et si bien qu'elles continuent de tracer des sillons dans notre esprit pour nous révéler l'envers de la fiction, l'examen impitoyable du réel à travers les mécanismes et outils de l'art du roman et aboutir à ce que j'aime à nommer la littérature obstinée. Dès Le Temps de Tamango, Boris installe une géographie poétique et littéraire qu'il n'a cessé d'approfondir depuis, à travers l'exploration de la mémoire menée à hauteur de justice. Avec ce premier roman, distingué par le Prix du Bureau sénégalais du droit d'auteur, Boris s'impose comme l'un des pionniers de la politique-fiction africaine et amorce la réflexion postcoloniale qui le poussera, des années plus tard, à écrire des essais comme L'Afrique au-delà du miroir et à entamer l'écriture en wolof. À travers une mise en abyme menée par des mécanismes de narration intradiégétiques et extradiégétiques, ce roman dépasse la question de la contestation et du roman des désillusions postindépendance. Les Tambours de la mémoire prolonge ce geste et s’inscrit dans la quête du héros national, pour déconstruire les idées reçues et les histoires adoptées ou livrées par l'ancien colon. Ce deuxième roman, à travers Fadel Sarr, hanté par des événements qu'il n'a pas lui-même vécus, fait de la mémoire une obsession qui précède l'individu et le dépasse. Il a obtenu en 1990 le Grand Prix de la République du Sénégal pour les lettres et, osons le dire, car les prix ne valent que par leurs lauréats, a conféré à cette distinction le prestige qui en fait le rêve de nombre d'écrivains sénégalais. Si tout le monde connaît Murambi et ce qu'il a mis en lumière, ce qu'il a dit du mal, de ses métamorphoses et de ses modes d'apparition, c'est dans deux autres textes qu'il faut chercher les réponses aux questions soulevées par ce roman : Kaveena et Le Cavalier et son ombre. Le Cavalier et son ombre, où Kadidja raconte des histoires à quelqu’un qu'elle ne voit jamais, dit comment la fable peut approcher l'horreur là où le témoignage seul échoue, ainsi que la condition de l’écrivain africain contemporain parlant à un peuple qui n’est pas le sien, qu’il ne voit pas et qu’il ne connaît pas. Kaveena, plongée dans les méandres de la néocolonialité, interroge le mal en tant que système, avec ses exécutants, ses commanditaires et ses silences. À travers l'écriture de ces deux textes, il prouve, si besoin en était, que le roman africain postcolonial n'a pas à choisir entre engagement politique et exigence formelle, que la mémoire collective et l'architecture narrative peuvent se renforcer mutuellement plutôt que se contredire. Ainsi, Boris ne cède dans ses textes ni à la tentation du reportage nu ni à celle de la métaphore esthétisante ; il creuse une autre voie entre fiction et archive historique, dans laquelle la littérature et le réel se contaminent et se déforment. En somme, ils sont chacun le miroir dans lequel est vu l'autre. Sans entrer dans d'autres considérations techniques ou génétiques de l'œuvre diopienne, et pour revenir à mon postulat de base, il vaut de noter le travail le plus important de Boris : mythifier le Sénégal, en faire une terre de littérature, et faire de son histoire et de ses blessures l'histoire de la littérature. En effet, sans citer in extenso tous les romans de Boris, on peut aisément voir combien, dans Le Cavalier et son ombre, Le Temps de Tamango, Les Petits de la guenon et Un tombeau pour Kinne Gaajo, le territoire sénégalais n'est pas un décor mais un organisme vivant, complexe, et le personnage le plus impactant. Les ruelles de Dakar, les rumeurs de quartier (de la Médina, par exemple), les saveurs et les odeurs des marchés, le crépuscule tombant ou le soleil se levant sur les contes constituent une géographie affective qui refuse l'exotisme autant que le folklore et mythifie le lieu dans sa banalité, en le rendant universel par un excès de précision locale. Ses romans labyrinthiques, où les récits s'enchâssent sans jamais se résoudre, où le conte traditionnel sert de matrice à une réflexion sur la folie, le meurtre, le pouvoir et la fabulation comme résistance au trauma et naissance d'une autre possibilité du réel, d'une autre Afrique postcoloniale glorieuse, se lisent de la même façon que son engagement politique et permettent de dire sans ambages que Boris est le Sénégal, car chacune des souffrances de son pays devient une obsession qu'on retrouve dans son œuvre et qu'il dénonce dans ses articles et tribunes politiques. Si l'on peut aisément croire que c'est l'ombre tutélaire de Cheikh Anta qui est à l'origine de la réappropriation de la langue entamée par Boris depuis une vingtaine d'années à travers l'écriture de ses textes en wolof, c'est surtout une autre leçon qu'il faut tirer de ce fait : l'appel de la souveraineté. Car un peuple qui ne sait pas sa propre langue, qui ne l'enseigne pas, qui n'apprend pas à ses enfants son histoire dans sa langue, est un peuple sans ancrage. Ce labyrinthe infini du nom de la pratique romanesque, que j'ai tenté de définir sommairement ici et dont Les Petits de la guenon représente peut-être l'accomplissement le plus abouti à ce jour, est la preuve matérielle de la raison pour laquelle Boris est le Sénégal, et dit pourquoi le Sénégal célèbre son fils. Dans ce roman, d'abord écrit en wolof sous le titre Doomi Golo, le vieux Nguirane Faye confie à des cahiers destinés à son petit-fils Badou, parti au loin, la mémoire d'un pays et d'un quartier : toute l'œuvre de Boris s'y retrouve, la transmission comme devoir, la langue comme ancrage, le récit comme rempart contre l'oubli. Cette littérature qui refuse l'amnésie, la facilité du récit consolant, et qui tient ouverte, dans la beauté précise et implacable de la prose, la question de ce que nous devons aux morts et aux vivants que la violence du monde a rendus invisibles, est le symbole de la veille entamée par Boubacar Boris Diop depuis plus de quarante ans, une veille qui nous interdit, en tant que nation, de dormir la conscience tranquille tant que subsiste à nos portes ne serait-ce qu’un moment d’injustice. S'il est un souhait à faire à ce passionné de Sartre — de l’œuvre duquel il a tiré son nom d’auteur et qui m’en a transmis la passion — pour son anniversaire, même s'il n'en a pas besoin, ce serait que l'Académie suédoise démontre sa modernité et s'inscrive résolument dans la littérature-monde en reconnaissant, dans la foulée du Prix Neustadt, ce fils devenu métaphore du Sénégal, qui est, pour beaucoup, dont moi-même, la plume la plus importante de la littérature contemporaine. Par Khalil DIALLO

items.title: Contrainte par corps : 26.000 personnes soustraites à la mesure
items.description: Devant la Chambre des conseillers, le ministre de la Justice a annoncé l’annulation de 22.315 avis de recherche et la libération de 3.991 détenus au titre de la contrainte par corps, tout en revendiquant 40.000 conciliations pénales. Interpellé ce mardi 27 octobre lors de la première séance de questions orales de la session d’octobre, Abdellatif Ouahbi a chiffré les effets des nouvelles dispositions du Code de procédure pénale sur deux dossiers sensibles : la contrainte par corps et la procédure de conciliation. Le ministre a présenté la démarche comme un effort mené avec le ministère public et la Sûreté nationale, afin que la contrainte par corps cesse de constituer un obstacle aux déplacements des citoyens et à leur liberté. Sur le premier volet, Abdellatif Ouahbi a fait savoir que des circulaires et des revues d’ensemble des avis de recherche avaient été diffusées, en particulier pour les personnes de moins de 20 ans ou de plus de 60 ans. Ce travail de vérification a débouché sur l’annulation de 22.315 avis de recherche, y compris dans d’autres situations où les conditions légales d’application de la mesure n’étaient plus réunies. Dans les établissements pénitentiaires, 3.991 personnes qui y étaient détenues à ce titre ont recouvré la liberté. Au total, a précisé le ministre, près de 26.000 personnes ont tiré profit de ces mesures, soit par l’annulation des avis de recherche émis à leur encontre, soit par une sortie de prison. Il a illustré les excès constatés par des cas de détention pour des sommes dérisoires, dont celui d’un homme incarcéré pour une dette n’excédant pas 80 dirhams, un exemple qui a poussé le département à intervenir pour mettre fin à cette situation et à fixer un nouveau plafond financier. Les amendements apportés au Code de procédure pénale interdisent désormais le recours à la contrainte par corps pour les dettes inférieures à 8.000 dirhams. Ils la limitent en outre aux personnes âgées de 20 à 60 ans, alors que l’âge minimal était jusque-là fixé à 18 ans. Le ministre s’est ensuite attardé sur le bilan de la conciliation, un mécanisme prévu par le nouveau code, dont les juges ont la faculté de se saisir et qui est appliqué depuis l’an dernier. Selon lui, la procédure a fait la preuve de son efficacité : depuis son entrée en application, 40.000 conciliations ont été réalisées, autant d’affaires qui auraient pu s’éterniser dans les couloirs des tribunaux et dans les prisons. La procédure repose sur le paiement d’une amende modeste, de 200 à 300 dirhams, destinée à clore des litiges mineurs comme les injures, les insultes ou les rixes. Les parties renoncent alors à leurs plaintes et le dossier est classé. Abdellatif Ouahbi a demandé aux conseillers d’imaginer le coût qu’aurait supporté l’État sans cette voie. Selon son estimation, 10.000 à 20.000 des 40.000 personnes concernées auraient fini en prison, où l’administration aurait dû pourvoir à leurs besoins pendant que leurs familles continuaient de souffrir à l’extérieur. Le ministre a enfin assuré que son département poursuivrait la recherche d’alternatives similaires aux peines privatives de liberté. À ses yeux, soustraire 40.000 citoyens au circuit judiciaire revient, en comptant leurs proches, à épargner une épreuve à 200.000 personnes. items.title: Fameye to light up ‘December in Juaben’ homecoming festival
items.description: Ghanaian musician Fameye is set to bring his music to Juaben this December as the annual “December in Juaben” homecoming festival returns with four days of entertainment, culture and community activities. Organised by the Richmond Amoateng Foundation, the festival will run from December 24 to 27, 2026, bringing residents, returning natives and visitors together under the theme, “Reconnecting Roots, Celebrating Heritage & Building Juabenman Together.” Fameye will perform alongside other artistes at the carnival night on December 26, with Adu Boaheng Park advertised as the venue. Seleka Shaker will be on DJ duties, while Highest MC will serve as hypeman. The performance forms part of a programme designed to make Juaben a destination for festive celebrations while strengthening connections between the town and its people. Activities begin on Thursday, December 24, with the arrival of guests and welcome activities. Christmas Day will feature a students’ party and football gala, creating an opportunity for young people to connect through entertainment and sport. A health walk and music festival follow on Saturday, December 26, before the celebrations conclude on Sunday, December 27, with “Dinner with Daasebre,” a special dinner gathering. Beyond the entertainment, the Richmond Amoateng Foundation says the annual initiative reflects a longer-term ambition to strengthen community identity, create opportunities and position Juaben as a vibrant cultural and tourism destination. For the foundation, the festival is an opportunity to bring culture, people and purpose together, with young people playing a central role in the community’s development. That vision gives the homecoming a significance beyond the Christmas calendar: a chance for those returning home to reconnect with their roots, renew relationships and contribute to conversations about Juaben’s future. The festival is expected to attract dignitaries, traditional rulers and other distinguished guests, who will be warmly welcomed by the Juabenmanhene, Nana Otuo Siriboe II, and the Juabenmanhemaa, Nana Akosua Akyamaa IV, alongside other community leaders. With Fameye on the bill and activities spanning music, sport, wellness and social gatherings, this year’s edition offers several reasons to make Juaben part of the December holiday itinerary. For sponsorship enquiries, organisers can be contacted on +233 55 391 2606 or +233 24 004 3747.

items.title: Government must take decisive and far-reaching action on Obuasi SHTS case – Methodist Church Ghana
items.description: The Methodist Church Ghana has called on the government to take decisive and far-reaching action on allegations of sexual abuse involving 19 female students of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS). The Church is demanding an independent and transparent investigation into the allegations against the school’s headmaster, Zakaria Abdulai, as well as accountability for any officials or institutions whose actions or inaction may have contributed to the alleged abuse. The allegations involving Obuasi SHTS have attracted national attention, with the number of students reportedly alleging abuse reaching 19. The school’s headmaster, Zakaria Abdulai, has been suspended by the Ghana Education Service pending investigation. The Ministry of Education has also directed the Criminal Investigations Department of the Ghana Police Service to investigate the allegations. Mr Abdulai is also reported to be the National Democratic Congress constituency secretary in Juaben and had been seeking to contest the constituency chairmanship. In a statement issued on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, and signed by its Gender, Family and Social Intervention Directorate, the Church condemned the alleged abuse and exploitation, expressing concern over the impact on the students and their families. “As a Church committed to the protection of children, the promotion of human dignity, and the pursuit of justice, we condemn in the strongest terms all forms of sexual abuse, exploitation, and violence against children and vulnerable persons,” the statement said. The Church stressed that schools must provide safe environments where students can learn and pursue their aspirations without fear of intimidation, abuse or victimisation. It expressed solidarity with the affected students and their families, calling for their healing and recovery, and commended those who had come forward to report the alleged abuse. The Methodist Church said the allegations raised broader questions about the effectiveness of child protection mechanisms within Ghana’s educational system. It expressed particular concern over reports that complaints may have been made over an extended period without adequate intervention. “Allegations that complaints may have been reported over an extended period without adequate intervention make the situation even more troubling,” the statement said. The Church argued that the case should prompt scrutiny not only of the alleged conduct of the headmaster but also of the systems intended to protect students from abuse. The Church outlined six measures it wants the government to pursue. These include a thorough, independent and transparent investigation into the allegations and any institutional failures connected to the case. It also called for the prosecution of anyone found culpable under Ghanaian law, regardless of their position or influence, and accountability for officials or institutions whose actions or inaction may have contributed to the alleged abuse. The Church further urged the government to provide the affected students and their families with confidential, professional and long-term psychological, medical, social and educational support. It called for stronger child protection and safeguarding systems across educational institutions, alongside confidential reporting mechanisms that allow students to report abuse without fear of retaliation. The Methodist Church urged state institutions, faith-based organisations, civil society groups, mental health professionals and community leaders to support the affected students and their families. It also appealed to the media and the public to respect the privacy and dignity of the students while supporting efforts to secure justice. “This painful episode must serve as a wake-up call to the nation. The safety and well-being of our children must never be compromised,” the statement said. PRESS RELEASE 2 Download

items.title: Mondial 2030 : la FIFA inspectera les stades marocains en novembre et décembre
items.description: La FIFA prévoit d’effectuer des visites d’inspection dans les villes candidates à l’organisation de la Coupe du monde 2030 au Maroc, en Espagne et au Portugal en novembre et décembre prochains. Cette étape doit permettre d’évaluer la conformité des stades aux exigences techniques et organisationnelles, avant l’arrêt de la liste définitive des enceintes retenues. Le Maroc entre dans une phase décisive des préparatifs du Mondial 2030. La Fédération internationale de football (FIFA) a annoncé, mardi 27 octobre, qu’une délégation se rendra dans les villes candidates du Maroc, de l’Espagne et du Portugal en novembre et décembre afin d’inspecter les stades susceptibles d’accueillir des rencontres de la compétition. Ces visites permettront d’évaluer l’état de préparation des infrastructures et leur conformité aux critères techniques et organisationnels exigés pour accueillir le plus grand rendez-vous du football mondial. Au Maroc, les inspections concerneront six villes : Agadir, Casablanca, Fès, Marrakech, Rabat et Tanger. Au Portugal, la délégation visitera Lisbonne et Porto. En Espagne, le programme prévoit des déplacements à Barcelone, Bilbao, Las Palmas, Madrid, Saint-Sébastien, Séville et Saragosse. La FIFA précise que d’autres stades pourraient être ajoutés au calendrier des visites. La liste définitive des stades retenus n’a pas encore été arrêtée. Le choix de l’enceinte qui accueillera la finale reste également en suspens, alors que le Maroc et l’Espagne sont en concurrence pour organiser cette rencontre phare. La répartition des matchs entre les différentes villes ne sera définie qu’après la validation de la liste finale des stades et des villes hôtes, ainsi que l’élaboration du calendrier de la compétition, a indiqué la FIFA. Le Mondial 2030 aura une dimension particulière puisqu’il marquera le centenaire de la première édition de la Coupe du monde, organisée en Uruguay en 1930. À cette occasion, les trois premiers matchs de la compétition se dérouleront en Argentine, en Uruguay et au Paraguay, avant la suite du tournoi organisée dans les trois pays hôtes principaux : le Maroc, l’Espagne et le Portugal. The post Mondial 2030 : la FIFA inspectera les stades marocains en novembre et décembre appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .
